title: Timeouts and retries
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Timeouts on every external call (Spring RestClient and WebClient, httpx), deadline budgets, retry rules, exponential backoff with jitter, retry amplification and idempotency.
source: Spring Framework RestClient and WebClient docs; Spring Retry; httpx timeouts docs; tenacity docs; AWS Builders Library (timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter); Google SRE book

questions.prompt: Create a RestClient whose underlying SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory has a connect timeout of 2 seconds and a read timeout of 5 seconds.

checks.label: builds the RestClient with the factory

questions.explanation: The JDK and most HTTP libraries default to no read timeout. With WebClient use .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) on the Mono plus Reactor Netty's responseTimeout and CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS options. Boot 3.4+ also has spring.http.client.connect-timeout and read-timeout properties.

questions.prompt: Create an httpx.AsyncClient named client with a default timeout of 5 seconds but a connect timeout of only 2 seconds, using httpx.Timeout.
questions.explanation: httpx applies a 5 second default for each of connect, read, write and pool if you set nothing, unlike requests, which waits forever. Remember that each timeout applies per phase, not to the whole request, so add an overall deadline (asyncio.timeout) too.

questions.prompt: Match each httpx timeout with the phase it limits.

right.text: Establishing the TCP (and TLS) connection to the server
Waiting for the next chunk of response data
Waiting to acquire a connection from the pool
Resolving the DNS cache entry TTL

questions.explanation: A slow trickle of bytes can reset a read timeout again and again, so an overall deadline is still needed.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In a call chain A -> B -> C, the timeout for the call from B to C should be shorter than the time A is still willing to wait for B.
questions.reason: Otherwise A gives up while B and C keep working on a result nobody will read, wasting capacity.

whys.a: Correct: nested calls need a shrinking deadline budget, otherwise work continues for an abandoned request.
whys.b: R is the reason behind A.

questions.explanation: Propagate a deadline (gRPC deadlines, an X-Request-Deadline header) and subtract elapsed time at each hop.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A client that times out waiting for a payment response cannot tell whether the server processed the payment.
questions.reason: A timeout means the server rolled back everything it did for the request.

whys.a: R is false so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: a timeout only says the client stopped waiting (A true); the server may have committed (R false).

questions.explanation: This is why mutating calls need idempotency keys: the client can retry safely or query the outcome.

questions.prompt: A call has a 2 second timeout, 3 attempts in total (1 original + 2 retries), and waits 1 s then 2 s between attempts. If every attempt times out, how many seconds pass before the caller gets the final error?
questions.explanation: 2 (attempt 1) + 1 (wait) + 2 (attempt 2) + 2 (wait) + 2 (attempt 3) = 9 seconds. Always compute the worst case and compare it with the caller's own timeout.

questions.prompt: Exponential backoff uses delay = base x 2^(n-1) for the n-th retry, with base 100 ms and no cap. What is the delay in milliseconds before the 5th retry?
questions.explanation: 100 x 2^4 = 1,600 ms. Delays run 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600. Real systems add a cap and jitter.

questions.prompt: Three services are chained: gateway -> orders -> inventory. Each layer makes up to 3 attempts per call (1 original + 2 retries) when the layer below fails. If inventory always fails, how many calls does inventory receive for one gateway request?
questions.explanation: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. This multiplication is why retries should happen at one layer only or be limited by a retry budget.

questions.prompt: Thousands of clients lost the same dependency at the same moment. Which retry delay strategy best avoids synchronised retry waves?

options.text: Exponential backoff with full jitter: sleep a random value from 0 up to the capped exponential delay.
options.why: Right: randomness spreads retries across the whole window.

options.text: Fixed delay of one second for every client.
options.why: All clients retry at the same instants, forming waves.
Clients that failed together retry together at 1, 2, 4 seconds.

options.text: Retrying immediately in a tight loop until success.
options.why: This maximises load on a recovering dependency and prevents recovery.

questions.explanation: The AWS Architecture Blog compared full, equal and decorrelated jitter; full jitter does the least total work. Add a retry budget on top.

questions.prompt: Which are sound retry rules for outbound calls? Select all that apply.

options.text: Retry only transient failures such as timeouts, connection resets, 503 and 429 (honour Retry-After).
Retry non-idempotent POSTs only when an idempotency key is sent.
options.why: Right: the key lets the server dedupe a request that actually succeeded.

options.text: Cap total retries with a budget, for example at most about 10 percent of requests.
options.why: Right: bounds the extra load retries can add.
These are caller errors that will fail the same way each time.

options.text: Retry at every layer of the call chain for maximum safety.
options.why: Retries multiply across layers and can crush the dependency.

questions.explanation: Retry at one layer (usually the outermost that has context), keep operations idempotent, and combine retries with a circuit breaker.

questions.prompt: Decorate fetch_price so it is retried up to 5 attempts in total, using exponential wait with jitter, only when httpx.TransportError is raised, and re-raises the last exception at the end. Use tenacity.
questions.starter: from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential_jitter, retry_if_exception_type
questions.model:
@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5), wait=wait_exponential_jitter(initial=0.5, max=10), retry=retry_if_exception_type(httpx.TransportError), reraise=True)
async def fetch_price(): ...
questions.explanation: tenacity supports async functions with the same decorator. Without reraise=True you get a RetryError wrapping the last exception. wait_random_exponential is another jittered option.

questions.prompt: Annotate a method fetchStock with Spring Retry so it runs at most 4 attempts in total on IOException, starting with a 200 ms delay that doubles each time.
questions.model:
@Retryable(retryFor = IOException.class, maxAttempts = 4, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 200, multiplier = 2))
public Stock fetchStock(String sku) throws IOException { ... }
questions.explanation: maxAttempts counts the original call. Needs @EnableRetry and a call through the Spring proxy (self-invocation bypasses it). Older versions spelled retryFor as include or value. Resilience4j @Retry(name = "x") is an equally valid answer in a Resilience4j project.

questions.text: Retries should use {1} backoff with {2} so clients do not retry in lockstep, and a retry {3} should cap the extra load that retries can add.
questions.explanation: Backoff spaces retries, jitter desynchronises clients, budget bounds amplification.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Exponential backoff alone prevents a thundering herd of synchronised retries.
questions.reason: Jitter randomises delays so that clients which failed together no longer retry at identical moments.

whys.d: Correct: without jitter, clients that failed together keep retrying together; jitter is the actual fix.

questions.explanation: Plain backoff only makes the waves less frequent, not less synchronised.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Retrying at every layer of a microservice chain multiplies the load on the lowest dependency.
questions.reason: Exponential backoff means that the delays double on each retry.

whys.a: Doubling delays do not cause the multiplication of calls.
whys.b: Correct: both true, but the multiplication comes from nested attempts, not from the doubling delays.

questions.explanation: Nested attempts multiply (3 x 3 x 3), delays add up. Both matter, for different reasons.

questions.prompt: True or false: an HTTP 400 Bad Request response is a good candidate for retry with exponential backoff.

options.why: The request itself is invalid, so it fails identically every time.
Right: 4xx caller errors are not transient; retry only timeouts, connection errors, 503 and 429.

questions.explanation: 408 and 429 are the usual 4xx exceptions. Classify errors into retryable and non-retryable before wiring a retry policy.
